name: J04 — the same journey, both clients, one product
about: Identical actions against the same running product: reach a place where a
prompt can be sent, compose one with a paste, send it, watch a real
external response stream, and interrupt a second one.
The ACTIONS are identical and the EXPECTATIONS are per client, because the
two clients draw different screens. A shared expectation would make one
client wait on the other's vocabulary, which measures nothing.
The retained client is entered with `i` on its opening project screen — the
runbook's route to the launch folder that does NOT bind a live fleet seat.
The oracle observation is explicit that only Grapt and the operator's own
identity may be navigated in the real registry, and this journey navigates
neither.
Timings are end to end and measured outside both clients. They compare a
felt experience; they do not attribute a difference to any one layer.
Observed and recorded rather than smoothed over: after `i` the retained
client goes STRAIGHT to a composer with the location's default agent and
model already applied, while the native client requires the user to choose a
model before a prompt is accepted. That is a real difference in steps and in
discoverability, and it is the point of comparing rather than a flaw in the
scenario. J01 requires the explicit selection, so the native behaviour is the
required one; the comparison records what it costs.
The reply wait counts occurrences PER CLIENT, because the reason for
counting is a property of one client's screen. The retained client draws no
marker that separates its transcript from its composer, and the composer
still holds the prompt — which contains the same words — so waiting for the
first occurrence would be satisfied by the client echoing back what was
typed, before the model had answered. The second occurrence is the reply.
The native client needs no such compensation: it prefixes transcript entries
with their role, so the awaited `[text] comparative canary` cannot match the
user's own `[you] ...` line and appears exactly once. Waiting for two was a
measurement fault of the first run — the reply was on screen, correct and
streamed, and the harness reported a timeout anyway.
INTERRUPTION is compared at the end, because it is the one action whose
cost is felt rather than measured: a client that takes two seconds to stop
a runaway answer is a different product from one that stops at once. The
request is deliberately long so there is something real to interrupt.
Only the native side asserts an interruption marker. The retained client's
a guess into an expectation would either fail for the wrong reason or, if I
guessed a substring that happens to appear, pass for the wrong reason. It
captures instead, and the expectation is added once the capture says what
the screen actually reads.
The streaming wait uses the same prefixed-marker discipline as the canary:
`STARTING` is asked for so the answer has a first word to wait on, the
native side waits for `[text] STARTING` which its own role prefix makes
unambiguous, and the retained side counts two because its transcript shows
the request as well. A bare digit would have matched anything already on
screen and passed before the model had said a word.
The request counts to two thousand because the first attempt did not: the
answer had ALREADY SETTLED before the interrupt landed — `durable
succeeded`, 406 output tokens — so `interrupted` could never appear and the
step measured nothing at all. There is also no capture between the marker
and the interrupt now, because that capture spent seconds of the very
streaming window the interrupt needs to land inside.
THE INTERRUPT COMPARES AN ACTION, NOT A KEYSTROKE, and an earlier revision
of this file got that wrong. It sent Ctrl+C to both clients and recorded
that the retained one exited — but Ctrl+C is that client's EXIT binding.
The frozen oracle is explicit: packages/tui/src/config/v1/keybind.ts has
app_exit `ctrl+c,ctrl+d,<leader>q` at :48, session_interrupt `escape` at
:96, and input_clear `ctrl+c` at :162. So the run had pressed quit and then
reported it as a failure to interrupt. Each client is now driven through
its own configured binding — Ctrl+C for the native client, Escape for the
retained one — and the same is done for leaving the client.
The stream must be OBSERVED ACTIVE before the interrupt, not assumed to be:
the first attempt interrupted a turn that had already settled (`durable
succeeded`, 406 output tokens), so nothing could be interrupted and the
step measured nothing. The answer counts to two thousand, and the native
side waits to see the execution still `running` before acting.
The native side waits on the RUNNING EXECUTION, not on a line of the
answer. A slice's label is a single row, and once the multi-line layout
landed a long answer scrolls its own `[text] STARTING` header out of the
transcript window within a poll or two — so waiting for it timed out while
the answer was on screen, counting, in front of the harness. The status
line says `running` for as long as the execution actually is, which is the
condition the interrupt needs and the one worth waiting on.
The request counts to three hundred rather than two thousand. At two
thousand the NATIVE side reported `durable failed` with the durable history
`incomplete (page whole, 1 unreadable)` while the retained client answered
the same request on the same product without complaint. That is a real
difference and it is being tracked as its own question; it is not the
interrupt, and leaving it inside this step would mean the interrupt
dimension could never be measured at all. Three hundred lines still streams
for long enough to be interrupted while genuinely running.
THE RETAINED INTERRUPT TAKES TWO PRESSES, and an earlier revision sent one
and called it done. The frozen implementation is explicit
(packages/tui/src/mini/footer.ts:960-979): the first press only ARMS,
showing `again to interrupt`, and a second press within five seconds fires
it. So a one-press scenario proved the binding existed and nothing about
the action completing — a `failure: null` from it was not interrupt parity.
What the three retained steps prove, precisely: the hint APPEARING proves
the first press registered and the client is armed; the second press lands
well inside the window (the harness sends it in under a second, so a
five-second timeout cannot explain what follows); the hint going AWAY
proves the armed state ended. Present-then-absent is a transition, which a
bare absence check would not be — that would pass against a client that had
never drawn the hint at all.
BOTH CLIENTS RUN THE SAME MODEL, and an earlier revision did not. The
native side took the first row of its picker — GPT-6 Astra — while the
retained side used the location's default, GPT-5.6 Sol. Every timing and
resource figure from that pairing describes two different models doing two
different pieces of work, so it cannot support a client comparison however
carefully it was measured.
The native picker is now filtered to `Sol` and the selection is verified on
BOTH sides before anything is compared. Selecting a model is not the same
as having selected it: the assertion is what makes this a controlled
comparison rather than a hope.
THE HINT GOING AWAY IS NOT THE INTERRUPT LANDING. `footer.ts:973-978`
clears the armed state and sets its notice BEFORE calling `onInterrupt`,
and the call is OPTIONAL, so a missing or failing callback would still
clear the hint and satisfy a check that stopped there.
ASSERT THE SURFACE THAT ACTUALLY SHIPS. An earlier revision waited for
`assistant interrupted` from `mini/entry.body.ts:214`. That module is not
the active frontend and the string never appears: an attended run sat in
timeout while the retained client was displaying its interrupt correctly.
Reading a plausible module is not reading the product.
The live route is `routes/session/index.tsx`. At 1518 it derives
`interrupted` from `props.message.error?.message === "Step interrupted"`,
at 1545-1546 it renders that as a trailing metadata word on the message
row, and at 1522 it SUPPRESSES the error box for that case — so an
interrupt is deliberately not shown as an error there.
The assertion is the metadata word rather than the `·` separator that
precedes it, to keep the expectation ASCII through the screen capture; the
separator adds no discrimination that the transition below does not
already provide.
THE NATIVE SIDE NEEDS THE SAME CARE, and it is asserted on the `saw` row
rather than on the settled outcome. An earlier revision of this file asked
for TWO occurrences of `interrupted`, reasoning that `view.rs:445` renders
the settled outcome as `<id> interrupted` and `view.rs:496` renders the
observation row as `saw <id> interrupted`, so two could only be both.
AN ATTENDED RUN REFUTED THAT, and the product was right. The settled row
read `durable failed` while the `saw` row was present, because after any
reconciliation the terminal comes from the DURABLE re-list, and the U3a
contract cannot say `interrupted`: `SessionMessageAssistantDtoFinish` has
stop / length / tool-calls / content-filter / error / unknown and no
interrupted member, and the assistant DTO carries no interrupted flag. So
`apply_durable` settles with NO execution id and a coarser outcome.
Refusing to paint that rebuilt terminal as the interrupt is DELIBERATE and
is itself witnessed: `a_stale_interrupt_never_resurrects_over_a_later
_terminal` in client/tests.rs exists because a revision that did carry the
interrupt across a rebuild would show a LATER execution's success as an
earlier one's interrupt. Absence cannot establish sameness.
So the honest native witness is the `saw` row, which `view.rs:494` renders
ONLY when `interrupted_observed` is set, and `projection.rs:389` sets that
ONLY from a live terminal whose outcome is `Interrupted`.
PRESENCE ALONE WOULD NOT BE ENOUGH, because `interrupted_observed` is set
and never cleared. A row left by an EARLIER interrupt would satisfy a bare
`expect` without this scenario interrupting anything, which is the stale
annotation the assertion has to exclude.
It is excluded by a TRANSITION rather than by presence. The row is asserted
ABSENT while this scenario's execution is confirmed `running`, and present
only after the interrupt key — so the row on screen at the end cannot be
one that predates the step, and something in between created it.
BOTH CLIENTS TAKE THAT TRANSITION, for the same reason. The retained word
is rendered per MESSAGE, so an interrupted turn earlier in the transcript
would satisfy a bare presence check just as a stale `saw` row would. Absent
while this execution runs and present after this interrupt is what makes it
THIS turn's interrupt on both sides.
That binds it to THIS execution. The only writer of the field is a live
terminal whose outcome is `Interrupted`, set in the SAME branch that
settles the execution and from the SAME observed id, and a terminal naming
an execution other than the running one is refused outright as
`TerminalAttributionMismatch`. Absent while THIS execution runs, present
after THIS interrupt, and unable to name any other execution: that is the
correlated live terminal, and it is the strongest claim this contract can
support without repainting durable history.
Likewise the model: a filter naming `Sol` proves a search box has text in
it. The SELECTION line — `model openai/GPT-5.6 Sol` — is what proves the
client is running that model, and it is asserted after the choice is made.

steps.paste: Reply with exactly: comparative canary. Do not use tools.
Reply with the word STARTING and then count slowly from one to three hundred, one number per line, with no other commentary.
